Water treatment processes for municipal supply follow a standardized sequence: (1) coagulation and flocculation (using aluminum sulfate, aka alum, or ferric chloride), (2) sedimentation (retention time typically 2-4 hrs), (3) filtration (sand, activated carbon, or membrane-based), and (4) disinfection (chlorination, UV irradiation, or ozonation). Raw water quality determines the specific configuration. Turbidity (measured in NTU, nephelometric turbidity units) must be reduced to below 1.0 NTU (preferably below 0.3 NTU) before disinfection is effective. Chlorine dosage is calculated based on chlorine demand plus a residual target (typically 0.2-0.5 mg/L free chlorine at the point of distribution). Emerging contaminants (e.g., PFAS, pharmaceuticals, microplastics) present challenges that conventional treatment trains were not designed to address. Advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) and granular activated carbon (GAC) adsorption show promise for PFAS removal (achieving 90%+ reduction in pilot studies). Infrastructure costs for upgrades range from $50M-$500M depending on plant capacity (measured in MGD, million gallons per day).
